title: Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries
abstract: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

I Introduction The proliferation of intelligent mobile devices and the Internet of Things (IoT) has accelerated the adoption of on-device federated learning (FL)—a decentralized machine learning paradigm that enables privacy-preserving model training directly on user devices [ 36 , 30 , 8 , 41 , 19 , 20 , 16 , 45 , 49 , 18 , 28 , 31 ] . By training locally without exposing raw data, FL addresses privacy concerns and is particularly attractive for resource-constrained environments such as smartphones, wearables, and edge networks. Despite its advantages, communication efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in FL, as participating devices often operate under stringent bandwidth and computation constraints [ 26 ] . To alleviate this issue, gradient compression techniques such as signSGD have been proposed, where model updates are quantized into compact one-bit representations [ 3 , 42 , 4 , 40 , 23 , 25 ] . While this approach significantly reduces communication cost, it also exposes individual gradient signs, making sign-based methods inherently vulnerable to inference attacks and privacy leakage [ 38 , 53 ] . Recent studies demonstrate that gradient signs can be exploited for gradient inversion and membership inference attacks [ 53 , 12 ] , highlighting the urgent need for end-to-end privacy protection even under extreme 1-bit quantization. Existing secure aggregation schemes have attempted to mitigate these vulnerabilities, but significant limitations remain. Approaches based on homomorphic encryption introduce prohibitive computational and communication overheads, rendering them unsuitable for resource-constrained edge or IoT environments. In addition, protocols that rely on preprocessed correlated randomness—such as Beaver triples or other MPC-style offline preprocessing [ 5 ] —incur substantial precomputation, storage, and communication costs, which further increase protocol complexity and limit practicality on lightweight devices [ 2 ] . Furthermore, most conventional secure aggregation frameworks are inherently incompatible with sign-based methods due to their structural mismatch. In particular, prior schemes assume linear aggregation over multi-bit gradients, whereas sign-based methods require a secure nonlinear majority voting operation which cannot be efficiently supported by conventional frameworks. A recent work, Hi-SAFE [ 24 ] , presents the first secure aggregation framework compatible with signSGD with majority vote ( signSGD-MV ), providing only computational security under cryptographic hardness assumptions while maintaining simple server-side aggregation and low latency through hierarchical subgrouping. However, it still depends on preprocessed Beaver triples, incurring offline overhead, and its additive secret sharing makes it vulnerable to user dropouts and adversarial behaviors—an important limitation in practical FL settings. To overcome these challenges, we focus on information-theoretic security , which guarantees privacy even against adversaries with unbounded computational power [ 10 ] . Unlike computational approaches, it is entirely independent of any computational hardness assumptions or heavy cryptographic mechanisms such as homomorphic encryption or correlated randomness. This unconditional protection relies solely on randomness and the algebraic properties of secret sharing, making it particularly suitable for lightweight and long-lived FL deployments where cryptographic assumptions or key management may not be practical. Building upon this foundation, we present a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework for sign-based FL. The core contribution lies in recognizing that the majority vote (MV) polynomial possesses a distinctive single-base structure —all monomials involve powers of a single aggregated value 𝐱 = ∑ i = 1 n 𝐱 i {\bf x}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\bf x}_{i} , where 𝐱 i {\bf x}_{i} is the one-bit gradient of user i i , rather than products of distinct inputs. This structural insight enables a fundamentally more efficient secure multiplication approach. We propose two complementary single-round secure multiplication methods. Method A (DN + Classical N N -BTE) handles general N N -input multiplication using an subset-mask table, suitable for small-scale settings. Method B (Single-Mask Power Sharing) exploits the single-base structure of MV polynomials: by employing a single random mask and the binomial expansion, offline computational complexity and storage are reduced from exponential to linear while requiring only a single online opening. Combined with the inverse-form exponent reduction that halves the polynomial degree, the proposed framework achieves up to 99.5% reduction in online communication and 85.7% reduction in latency compared to the conventional Beaver-triple-based approaches. Furthermore, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding properties of the secure multiplication, the proposed framework attains strong robustness against both user dropouts and adversarial corruptions, improving practical FL accuracy by up to 20.65% and 10.74% under dropout and adversarial conditions , respectively. Only the final majority vote is revealed to the server, ensuring end-to-end privacy with minimal communication overhead. I-A Contributions The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • Lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation. We propose a lightweight secure aggregation framework that ensures information-theoretic privacy under the honest-majority assumption, without relying on any computational hardness assumptions or heavy cryptographic mechanisms. It remains secure against computationally unbounded adversaries, making it suitable for long-lived, resource-constrained FL deployments. • End-to-end privacy via secure MV polynomial evaluation. The framework securely evaluates MV polynomials for sign-based FL, revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server and preventing inference from intermediate gradient signs. • Inverse-form exponent reduction. We introduce an algebraic transformation that rewrites high-degree terms as inverse powers, halving the maximum polynomial degree and further reducing both communication and computational costs. • Single-round secure multiplication. We propose two single-round secure multiplication methods that enable secure evaluation of MV polynomials, thereby achieving end-to-end privacy: (i) Method A (DN + N N -BTE): A two-layer method where Layer 1 performs DN-style binary multiplications and Layer 2 aggregates results via the classical N N -BTE. It achieves single-round latency with low online communication cost, but requires exponential offline computational complexity and storage. (ii) Method B (Single-Mask Power Sharing): A structure-aware method that exploits the single-base structure of MV polynomials. Using a single mask and the binomial theorem, it achieves single-round latency , linear offline computational complexity and storage, with minimal online communication —only a single field element per user. • Robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors. By exploiting the inherent MDS-code properties of secure multiplication, the proposed framework achieves robustness against both user dropouts and malicious participants, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. I-B Organization The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on secure aggregation and communication-efficient federated learning. Section III provides background on secure multiplication and recent advancements relevant to our work. Section IV presents the system model and problem formulation, and Section V details the proposed framework and its design components. Sections VI and VII provide theoretical analysis and experimental results, respectively, and Section VIII concludes the paper with discussions on practical implications and future research directions. II Related Work Secure aggregation has been widely investigated in FL. Masking-based protocols [ 5 , 44 ] rely on pairwise secret sharing, but partial information may leak under semi-honest settings. Differential privacy (DP) techniques [ 46 , 7 , 34 ] provide formal privacy guarantees, yet typically require strong noise that degrades accuracy. Homomorphic encryption (HE) approaches [ 50 , 11 , 22 , 35 , 9 , 6 , 13 ] achieve strong security, but they incur high computational cost and remain inefficient for nonlinear operations such as sign-based aggregation. Communication-efficient schemes such as signSGD and signSGD-MV [ 3 ] reduce uplink traffic to one bit per parameter, but revealing raw gradient signs causes severe privacy leakage. Moreover, most existing secure aggregation frameworks are not directly compatible with such sign-based methods. Hi-SAFE [ 24 ] is the first secure aggregation framework compatible with signSGD-MV , providing computational security based on cryptographic hardness assumptions while maintaining simple server-side aggregation and low latency through hierarchical subgrouping. Nevertheless, it relies on preprocessed Beaver triples, which incur high offline overhead, and its additive secret sharing makes it vulnerable to user dropouts and adversarial behaviors—limitations that remain critical in practical FL environments. In contrast, our work introduces a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework , which removes heavy offline requirements while providing information-theoretic security under the honest-majority setting. The key insight is exploiting the single-base structure of MV polynomials, which enables linear offline computational complexity and storage—a dramatic improvement over exponential alternatives. Moreover, by leveraging the inherent MDS-code properties of the proposed secure multiplication, the framework attains robustness against both user dropouts and adversarial behaviors. Altogether, the proposed framework yields a more scalable and resilient foundation for secure aggregation in FL. The comparison considers multiple criteria including the type of security guarantee, exposure level to the server, accuracy preservation, and overall communication and computational efficiency. In particular, masking-based approaches expose intermediate summation values during MV computation, and DP schemes suffer from accuracy degradation due to the addition of noise. While masking provides dropout resilience and adversarial robustness, it does not support full recovery of dropped shares or correction of corrupted values as our framework does—it only tolerates such failures without restoring the exact aggregation result. Similarly, DP offers dropout resilience but cannot correct adversarial corruptions. HE [ 9 ] , while cryptographically strong and post-quantum secure, remains computationally intensive and is inefficient for nonlinear operations such as majority vote. Hi-SAFE [ 24 ] achieves computational security through Beaver-triple–based aggregation and reveals only the final majority vote to the server. However, it lacks dropout recovery and adversarial robustness. In contrast, the proposed method achieves information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption and exploits the single-base structure of MV polynomials to achieve linear offline complexity and high communication efficiency. By leveraging the inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework enables full recovery of dropped user contributions and complete correction of adversarial corruptions within the decoding threshold, providing strong robustness without any accuracy degradation. Furthermore, all secure computations are performed in a single round, resulting in extremely low latency and high overall communication efficiency. Consequently, the proposed framework establishes a fully secure and resilient aggregation foundation for sign-based FL with information-theoretic privacy guarantees. III Preliminaries In this section, we briefly recall cryptographic building blocks relevant to our protocol design. III-A Beaver Triple Extension for N N -Fan-in Multiplication A Beaver triple [ 1 ] is a standard tool for secure MPC, enabling multiplication over secret-shared values without revealing private inputs. A Beaver triple ( 𝐚 , 𝐛 , 𝐜 ) ∈ 𝔽 p ({\bf a},{\bf b},{\bf c})\in\mathbb{F}_{p} satisfies 𝐜 = 𝐚 ⋅ 𝐛 ( mod p ) {\bf c}\!=\!{\bf a}\!\cdot\!{\bf b}\!\pmod{p} , where 𝐚 , 𝐛 , 𝐜 {\bf a},{\bf b},{\bf c} are secret-shared between two parties P 0 P_{0} and P 1 P_{1} . Precomputed Beaver triples enable each binary secure multiplication to be performed in a single online round of interaction, after the correlated random Beaver triples ( 𝐚 , 𝐛 , 𝐜 ) ({\bf a},{\bf b},{\bf c}) are sufficiently generated during the offline phase. y}\rrbracket_{0},\llbracket{\bf y}\rrbracket_{1} III-B ATLAS Multiplication ATLAS [ 15 ] is an information-theoretically secure MPC protocol that improves both communication and round complexities under the honest-majority assumption ( t < n / 2 t<n/2 ), where t t is the maximum number of colluding or corrupted parties. While DN method [ 10 ] is simple and robust, its round and communication costs limit scalability for deep multiplication chains. ATLAS introduces two orthogonal optimizations: • Communication reduction. By using t t -wise independent randomness, only t t random double sharings need to be uniformly random, while the rest are derived via a hyper-invertible matrix. This amortizes the preprocessing cost and reduces total communication cost. • Round reduction. By forcing an output of DN multiplication into a Beaver-triple–friendly form, ATLAS allows Beaver triples for the next layer to be prepared in parallel. As a result, two consecutive layers of parallel multiplications can be evaluated in one reconstruction round, halving the number of rounds. Two-Layer Evaluation ATLAS efficiently evaluates two layers of multiplications by combining DN-style masking in the first layer with binary Beaver triples in the second layer as in Algorithm 2 . III-C Construction of MV Polynomials via Fermat’s Little Theorem Fermat’s Little Theorem is a cornerstone of number theory with significant implications in cryptography, modular arithmetic, and secure computation [ 43 ] . It provides an efficient means to simplify large exponentiations modulo a prime, which is particularly advantageous for constructing indicator functions over finite fields. Indicator Function via Fermat’s Little Theorem Formally, if p p is a prime and a a is an integer such that a ≢ 0 ( mod p ) a\not\equiv 0\pmod{p} , then a p − 1 ≡ 1 ( mod p ) . a^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod{p}. From this, an indicator function over 𝔽 p \mathbb{F}_{p} can be derived: for x , a ∈ 𝔽 p x,a\in\mathbb{F}_{p} , 𝟙 { x = a } = 1 − ( x − a ) p − 1 ( mod p ) = { 1 , if ​ x = a , 0 , otherwise . \mathds{1}_{\{x=a\}}=1-(x-a)^{p-1}\!\!\pmod{p}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }x=a,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (1) This compact formulation is particularly useful for mapping discrete decision rules into polynomial form, enabling efficient precomputation and evaluation in secure majority-vote aggregation [ 24 ] . IV-A 1 Standard FL Framework Typical FL algorithms proceed in synchronized communication rounds, consisting of local updates followed by global aggregation. In each global round τ \tau , the server randomly selects a subset 𝒮 τ ⊆ [ N t ] {\cal S}_{\tau}\subseteq[N_{t}] of n n active users [ 37 ] . Let C = n N t C=\frac{n}{N_{t}} be the ratio of active users who participate in each global round. Each active user performs local updates with its own data and sends the updated model back to the server. The de-facto algorithm of FL is FedAvg [ 37 ] , which operates as follows: • (Downlink transmission) The server samples n n active users from all N t N_{t} users (i.e., 𝒮 τ ⊆ [ N t ] {\cal S}_{\tau}\subseteq[N_{t}] with | 𝒮 τ | = n |{\cal S}_{\tau}|=n ) and broadcasts the current model 𝜽 ​ ( τ ) \hbox{$\theta$}(\tau) to them. • (Local update) Each user i ∈ 𝒮 τ i\in{\cal S}_{\tau} sets 𝜽 i ​ ( τ ) = 𝜽 ​ ( τ ) \hbox{$\theta$}_{i}(\tau)=\hbox{$\theta$}(\tau) and updates its local model via SGD: 𝜽 i ​ ( τ + 1 ) = 𝜽 ​ ( τ ) − η ​ 𝐠 i ​ ( τ ) \hbox{$\theta$}_{i}(\tau+1)=\hbox{$\theta$}(\tau)-\eta{\bf g}_{i}(\tau) , where 𝐠 i ​ ( τ ) = ∇ f i ​ ( 𝜽 ​ ( τ ) ) {\bf g}_{i}(\tau)=\nabla f_{i}(\hbox{$\theta$}(\tau)) and η > 0 \eta>0 is the learning rate. • (Uplink transmission) Each user i ∈ 𝒮 τ i\in{\cal S}_{\tau} sends the updated local information 𝜽 i ​ ( τ + 1 ) \hbox{$\theta$}_{i}(\tau+1) to the server. • (Global update) From the aggregated information { 𝜽 i ​ ( τ + 1 ) : i ∈ 𝒮 τ } \{\hbox{$\theta$}_{i}(\tau+1):i\in{\cal S}_{\tau}\} , the server updates the global model via the weighted average: 𝜽 ​ ( τ + 1 ) = ∑ i ∈ 𝒮 τ m i ​ 𝜽 i ​ ( τ + 1 ) ∑ i ∈ 𝒮 τ m i \hbox{$\theta$}(\tau+1)=\frac{\sum_{i\in{\cal S}_{\tau}}m_{i}\hbox{$\theta$}_{i}(\tau+1)}{\sum_{i\in{\cal S}_{\tau}}m_{i}} . This assumption naturally aligns with signSGD-MV , which relies on the majority of users providing correct local signs; if t ≥ n / 2 t\geq n/2 , the global majority vote itself becomes incorrect. Thus, the honest-majority setting is both a natural and essential condition for ensuring correctness and privacy. These assumptions provide the foundation for our proposed secure aggregation framework. In the following section, we present two complementary methods that achieve information-theoretic security under these assumptions while minimizing online communication costs and latency. V Proposed Secure Aggregation Methods This section presents two complementary components that together enable efficient and information-theoretically secure evaluation of MV polynomials in FL, ensuring end-to-end privacy by revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. Unlike prior approaches that rely solely on binary Beaver triples or DN-style multiplication [ 1 , 10 , 15 ] , the proposed framework introduces new primitives that jointly achieve substantial reduction in communication cost and latency , while keeping preprocessing and storage manageable. (i) Inverse-Form Exponent Reduction. We introduce an inverse-form polynomial construction that halves the maximum exponentiation depth . This transformation reduces the number and depth of secure multiplications required to evaluate the MV polynomial, leading to lower communication and computational costs without affecting accuracy or security. The reduced degree also enables scalable, single-round secure polynomial evaluation. (ii) Single-Round Secure Multiplication. To realize one-round secure multiplications, we propose two realizations, Method A and Method B, under a unified DN-based architecture, each targeting different multiplication structures: • Method A (DN + N N -BTE). This method adopts a two-layer structure: Layer 1 performs DN-style masked openings for binary multiplications, and Layer 2 aggregates the results using the classical N-BTE, enabling secure computation of the product of all pairwise multiplications within one round under an honest-majority setting. However, it requires an exponential subset-mask table of size 2 N − N − 1 2^{N}{-}N{-}1 , resulting in Θ ​ ( N ⋅ 2 N ) \Theta(N\cdot 2^{N}) offline DN multiplications and O ​ ( 2 N ) O(2^{N}) storage. While Method A minimizes online latency, its scalability is limited by the exponential offline cost. • Method B (Single-Mask Power Sharing). For MV polynomial evaluation, Method B exploits the special structure where all multiplications involve powers of a single aggregated value 𝐱 k {\bf x}^{k} rather than products of distinct inputs. Using a single mask 𝐚 {\bf a} and the binomial theorem, Method B achieves linear O ​ ( N ′ ) O(N^{\prime}) offline computation and storage, where N ′ = ( p − 1 ) / 2 N^{\prime}\!=\!(p\!-\!1)/2 is the maximum polynomial degree after inverse-form exponent reduction. This approach preserves the single-round online phase and honest-majority security while dramatically reducing overhead compared to Method A. Next, a secure aggregation framework is proposed, which combines (i) inverse-form exponent reduction for lower multiplicative depth and (ii) single-round secure multiplication tailored to MV polynomial evaluation. Together, they achieve efficient, one-round, and information-theoretically secure aggregation suitable for large-scale federated learning.
